name: Is this prompt an engineering choice?
note: Each scenario contrasts a casual prompt with a disciplined one. Predict what actually makes it robust before you reveal it.

items.prompt: Prompt A: "Summarize this."  Prompt B: "Summarize the email below in 2 sentences for a busy executive; if it names a deadline, state the date."  Which is the engineering choice?
candidates: B — it pins length, audience, and an explicit rule for the edge case (a deadline), so outputs are consistent and testable
They're equivalent; the model infers the rest
B over-specifies and will confuse the model
items.correct: B — it pins length, audience, and an explicit rule for the edge case (a deadline), so outputs are consistent and testable
items.explanation: A under-specifies, so every call drifts on length, tone, and edge cases. B encodes the spec — length, audience, and a conditional for the deadline — turning a vague ask into something repeatable and checkable. A prompt is a spec, not a wish.
items.principle: Specify length, audience, format, and the edge cases — or the model decides them for you.

items.prompt: You extract {name, amount, due_date} from invoices to feed a database. The prompt says "tell me the name, amount, and due date." What breaks first in production?
candidates: Free-form prose can't be parsed reliably — you need a structured-output contract (a JSON schema) plus validation
The model can't actually read invoices
You need a bigger context window
Nothing — prose output is fine to parse
items.correct: Free-form prose can't be parsed reliably — you need a structured-output contract (a JSON schema) plus validation
items.explanation: Prose answers vary in wording and order, so the downstream parser breaks on the first unusual phrasing. Ask for a fixed JSON schema and validate it (reject or repair on a miss). Structured output is what turns an LLM call into a reliable function call.
items.principle: If code consumes the output, demand a schema and validate it — don't parse prose.

items.prompt: A prompt works perfectly on the three test emails you tried, so you ship it. Why isn't that evidence it's robust?
candidates: Three happy-path examples don't cover the distribution — you need a held-out test set and versioned prompts to catch regressions
Three is an unlucky number; try a fourth
It is evidence — if it works, ship it
You should fine-tune the model instead
items.correct: Three happy-path examples don't cover the distribution — you need a held-out test set and versioned prompts to catch regressions
items.explanation: A prompt that passes three hand-picked cases tells you nothing about the long tail: empty input, two deadlines, a different language, a hostile user. Treat prompts like code — a held-out eval set, version control, and a regression check whenever you edit. "Worked once" is a demo, not a test.
items.principle: Prompts are code: version them and test them against a held-out set, not three happy-path examples.
